headline: Skyroot lifts off. NASA cuts losses. SpaceX waits.
deck: This week, India's Skyroot Aerospace celebrates a successful launch while NASA terminates a lunar lander project.

stories.head: Skyroot's Vikram-1 rockets to orbit successfully
stories.body: Skyroot Aerospace achieved a major milestone with the Vikram-1 rocket reaching orbit on its inaugural flight. This success positions India as a competitive player in the commercial launch market, especially as global demand for affordable access to space increases. Now, the challenge is maintaining this momentum without a costly misstep.
stories.soWhat: If Skyroot can replicate this success, they'll attract serious investment and partnerships, but one failure could derail their progress.

stories.head: NASA pulls Draper lunar lander funding
stories.body: NASA has officially terminated the Draper lunar lander mission due to ongoing development delays, reallocating resources to more promising projects. This decision underscores the agency's shift towards prioritizing efficiency and timely deliverables over ambitious but stalled initiatives. The termination also frees up approximately $100 million for future endeavors.
stories.soWhat: This isn't just a setback for Draper; it’s a warning shot for contractors that NASA's patience is wearing thin in a budget-constrained environment.

stories.head: SpaceX's IPO signals mainstream acceptance
stories.body: SpaceX's impending IPO, valued at $470 billion, marks a significant milestone for the space industry, indicating that the sector is now firmly entrenched in capital markets. With investors eager to back space ventures, the stakes are rising, and the pressure is on for SpaceX to deliver consistent performance. This could lead to more companies following suit, eyeing public offerings.
stories.soWhat: If SpaceX stumbles post-IPO, it could sour investor sentiment across the broader space sector, which is still finding its footing.

watchlist.title: Watch for further Skyroot developments
watchlist.body: Skyroot's next steps will be crucial in determining whether they can sustain their recent success and attract further investment.

watchlist.title: NASA's next lunar mission plans
watchlist.body: With Draper's exit, NASA will need to pivot quickly to ensure its lunar ambitions remain on track.

watchlist.title: SpaceX's IPO impact on competitors
watchlist.body: The ramifications of SpaceX's IPO could reverberate through the entire space industry, influencing funding and valuations.

watchlist.title: True Anomaly's Series C implications
watchlist.body: True Anomaly's $190 million Series C round highlights growing interest in co-orbital security, a sector that may see increased defense spending.

talent.statLabel: Job orders YoY · plus 2 starters per head, an 8-year first
talent.head: Demand has doubled. So has our hit rate.
talent.body: EVONA's job orders are up 2.0× year-over-year, and for the first time in our eight-year history we're placing two new starters per EVONA staff member. The first number says demand is real. The second says we're converting it, which in recruitment is the only number that actually matters. Growth is heaviest in Series B/C startups; primes are running flat. Compensation isn't the variable. The constraint is schedule risk in the primes: senior engineers leave Boeing, Lockheed, Northrop because they want to ship hardware before retirement.
